newsitem.title: USA: IEA to voice concern on smaller U.S. oil reserve.
newsitem.headline: IEA to voice concern on smaller U.S. oil reserve.

text.p: The International Energy Agency was set to warn the United States that it was concerned that U.S. oil imports were rising while its government-held reserves have dropped.

"It is therefore a matter of considerable concern to the Agency that, while U.S. net oil imports have steadily risen to some 50 percent of consumption, the import coverage of the SPR (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) has fallen from 90 days to less than 70 days," John Ferriter, IEA deputy executive director, said in remarks prepared for a Senate Energy Committee hearing Tuesday.

"The requirements of energy security necessitate that the IEA countries maintain and if possible increase their emergency oil reserves, and remain ready to use them, in coordination with other IEA countries, at the appropriate time," Ferriter said.
Emergency stocks of IEA members -- 24 oil importing countries -- have dropped to the lowest level since 1986, representing a loss of about three weeks of import supply protection, he said.
Given current ample supplies and relatively low oil prices, Ferriter said it is easy to be complacent about the world's energy situation.

But he said the increasing use of oil in the transportation sector, where it is difficult to substitute other fuels and where responses to market changes are quick, would worsen economic consequences of a supply disruption.
He also cited forecasts for oil importing nations' growing dependence on supplies from the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

Markets must be convinced that governments will use their strategic stocks in the face of a serious disruptions, or oil consumers and large consumers will build up their own stocks in a crisis, and aggravate shortages, he said.
Ferriter also said the IEA supported pending legislation that would provide anti-trust protections for industry advice or information on drawing down SPR stocks.
IEA Director Robert Priddle last summer said he was concerned by the $1.145 billion sale of SPR oil proposed in President Clinton's budget plan for 2002 to help reduce the budget deficit.

About $550 million worth of oil has been sold from the SPR over the last few years, with part of that to cover costs of closing an SPR storage facility that had a potential to leak, and the rest to generate revenue for other programs or to help reduce the deficit.
The Energy Department is doing an analysis on how best to manage the SPR, or even whether it should be maintained. That analysis is due this fall.

The Energy Committee hearing was to be on legislation that would extend the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which oversees the SPR program. The committee also was considering a bill to allow the Energy Department to lease unused SPR storage capacity, and other bill to require that all revenue from leasing facilities be used to buy more oil for the SPR.
